chief_complaint: 7 days of fever, chills, headache and a dry cough.
history_of_present_illness: He developed slide-positive falciparum malaria whilst living in southern Laos and was treated with intravenous infusions and intramuscular artemether 80 mg for 5 days, which he had brought from China as standby therapy, but did not improve. The fever persisted, jaundice developed and he was therefore transferred to the capital Vientiane.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a Chinese itinerant trader who developed falciparum malaria whilst living in southern Laos, and he could have contracted other common infectious diseases in Laos.
vitals: On admission he was febrile (39.5°C, 103.1°F) with normal blood pressure and Glasgow Coma Score.
physical_exam: He had nausea, dry cough, moderate dehydration, chest pain and abdominal tenderness. His chest was clear and no hepatosplenomegaly was detected.
labs_and_diagnostics: Giemsa smear was negative for malaria parasites but a rapid diagnostic test (HRP-2) was positive for Plasmodium falciparum, consistent with recent falciparum malaria. Serum creatinine and glucose were normal. Laboratory results showed ALT 301 U/L (reference range <40), AST 230 U/L (reference range <37), ALP 470 U/L (reference range <120), Total bilirubin 14 µmol/L (reference range <14.5), and Direct bilirubin 6.4 µmol/L (reference range <4.3). His blood smear was negative, but his rapid diagnostic test was positive for P. falciparum.
differential_diagnosis: The most important differential diagnoses include bacterial co-infection, especially with Salmonella species, other common infectious diseases contracted in Laos such as scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi), murine typhus (Rickettsia typhi), leptospirosis, tuberculosis or dengue fever. Other possibilities include artemisinin-resistant falciparum malaria, incorrect dosing of artemether, poor quality artemether, or issues with intestinal absorption of the medicine.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was initially treated with intravenous infusions and intramuscular artemether 80 mg for 5 days but did not improve. Upon transfer, he was treated with oral quinine sulphate 10 mg/kg every 8 hours and doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours for 7 days. His fever cleared 35 hours after starting this therapy and he was discharged well, with no evidence found for any other infections. Investigation revealed that the suspect artemether sample contained only 59 mg (74% of stated on the vial), indicating it was substandard due to inadequate active ingredient, which, combined with underdosing and inadequate duration, most likely resulted in the poor clinical response.
final_diagnosis: The patient's persistent fever and jaundice were ultimately diagnosed as falciparum malaria that failed to respond to initial treatment due to the use of substandard artemether. This was supported by the negative Giemsa smear but positive HRP-2 RDT for Plasmodium falciparum, elevated liver enzymes and direct bilirubin, and the resolution of symptoms after appropriate treatment with oral quinine sulphate and doxycycline. Laboratory analysis of the initial artemether revealed it contained only 74% of the stated active ingredient, leading to underdosing and clinical failure.

images.caption: Examples of genuine (A) and falsified (B) artemether-lumefantrine discovered in Africa. The red circles indicate errors made by the criminals. The falsifiers confused 'm' with 'rn' in 'lagern' (German for "storing") and printed the packets with the word 'lagem' in error. The falsified samples contained no detectable artemether or lumefantrine but did contain subtherapeutic pyrimethamine. (Reproduced from Newton, P.N., Green, M.D., Mildenhall, D.C., et al., 2011. Poor quality vital anti-malarials in Africa - an urgent neglected public health priority. Malar J. 10, 352.)
